latin.262:
§. III.
Ex utroque Obicum Fonte alii aliique Rivuli, consimilem aquam trahentes, deducuntur, Autori nostro notati.
latin.263: Ex Priori (1.) Errorem quemvis, in haeresin pro libidine vertere, vel dissensum minoris momenti, in fundamentalem; In fundamentalem, inquam, quando vel omnino fictus est dissensus eoque nullus, vel Verbalis tantùm, vel ad summum, Modum rei concernens.
latin.264: (2.) Haeresi practica laborare, i. e. Charitatis judicio nullum locum relinquere, omniaque à dissentientibus dicta in pessinam quamque partem interpretari.
latin.265: Ex posteriori [1.] Sensu suô abundare, novitates suas bonâ fide aliis instillare, in Ecclesiae Pacisque Ecclesiasticae praejudicium.
latin.266: (2.) Adiaphoris Ecclesiasticis, ob inolitam consuetudinem, pertinaciter, etiam ubi periculum peccandi est, itemque cum apertissima adversus Magistratum Superiorem inobedientia, per Zelum, ignorantiae debitum, inhaerere.
latin.267: Plura collige ex Ramo Olivae Septentrionalis Joh. Matthaei Stregensis Episcopi, Bacca quartâ, Sexta, Septima & Octava.

pass_a.262: §. III. From either Fountain of the Obstacles other and still other Rivulets, drawing like water, are led down, noted by our Author.
pass_a.263: From the Prior (1.) To turn any Error into heresy at will, or a dissent of lesser moment into a fundamental one; into a fundamental one, I say, when the dissent is either entirely feigned and so none, or only Verbal, or at most concerns the Mode of the thing.
pass_a.264: (2.) To labor under practical heresy, i.e. to leave no place for Charity’s judgment, and to interpret everything said by dissenters in the worst possible part.
pass_a.265: From the posterior [1.] To abound in one’s own Sense, and in good faith to instill one’s novelties into others, to the prejudice of the Church and of Ecclesiastical Peace.
pass_a.266: (2.) To cling obstinately to Ecclesiastical Adiaphora because of ingrained custom, even where there is danger of sinning, and likewise with most open disobedience against the Superior Magistrate, through a Zeal owed to ignorance.
pass_a.267: Collect more from the Northern Olive-branch of John Matthew, Bishop of Strängnäs — the Fourth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Berry.

262: §. III. From either fountain of these obstacles still other rivulets run down, drawing the same kind of water — ones our Author notes.
263: From the first fountain: (1.) Stretch any error into heresy at will, or turn a lesser dissent into a fundamental one.
“Fundamental,” I mean, when the dissent is wholly feigned and so none at all, or only verbal, or at most about the mode of the thing.
264: (2.) Labor under practical heresy — leave no room for charity’s judgment, and take everything dissenters say in the worst possible sense.
265: From the second fountain: [1.] Swell with your own sense, and in good faith drip your novelties into others — to the hurt of the church and of church peace.
266: (2.) Cling stubbornly to church adiaphora from long habit, even where sin is a real risk,
and even with open disobedience to the higher magistrate, under a zeal that is really owed to ignorance.
267: Gather more from the Northern Olive-branch of Johannes Matthiae, Bishop of Strängnäs — berries four, six, seven, and eight.
Stop before Annotatio V (Limites Consociationis Ecclesiasticae).
